sent.t: There's a piece of paper in my wallet, folded in four, soft at the creases, and I have been carrying it for 11 years.
It's my funeral.
Four lines and a number at the bottom, $4,810.
I buried close to 7,000 people in 40 years.
I started at 13, sweeping the chapel floor for my father in Enelco, Guadalajara.
Then 25 years on the west side of San Antonio, Guadalupe Street, Zarzamora, Comers.
And I can tell you the one thing 40 years does to a man.
It takes away the mystery.
I know what a funeral cost.
I know what is worth.
And I know exactly which parts I want for myself and which parts I will not pay for, not with my wife's money, not with my
son's.
Today I'm going to read you that paper, line by line, with the prices in dollars, straight off the price list I keep in my desk,
and I'm going to tell you about the morning of November 3rd, 1999, when my father told me what he wanted for his own funeral, walking
out of the Panteón de Mezquitán with the Cempasúchil still yellow on the ground.
I kept what he said.
Four years later, I buried him exactly that way.
And that is the reason I wrote my four lines.
By tonight, you'll have yours.
Not because I'm selling you something.
I don't sell anything anymore.
Because there is a piece of paper you can write in 20 minutes that saves your family about $6,000 and one very bad week.
Line one, the box.
Here's what nobody explains at the arrangement table.
The casket is the biggest line on the bill and it is the least important thing in the room.
I have watched families spend $8,000 on a casket and then ask me, whispering, if we can do the service on a Tuesday because the money ran
out.
The funeral rule in this country, the FTC funeral rule, federal law since 1984, says the funeral home has to give you a written casket price
list, and they have to give it to you when you walk in before they show you anything, not after.
And it says something else, and this is the part they don't say out loud.
You can buy a casket somewhere else, and the funeral home cannot charge you a handling fee for it.
That's in the rule.
16 CFR, Part 453.
If they tell you there's a fee, they're breaking the law, and you can call the FTC and say so.
The casket I want is a cloth-covered particle board box, solid, square.
It seals with a simple gasket.
It holds 190 pounds of a man who ate too much pan dulce.
And it costs $1,195.
Same box the funeral home buys for $600 and marks up.
And here's the other thing.
Every funeral home will offer you a protective casket, Rubber gasket, locking mechanism, sometimes a warranty that says it will not let water in.
$600, sometimes $900 more.
I have opened graves at 10 years.
I'll tell you about that in the next video.
That gasket did not protect anything.
What it does is hold the moisture inside.
The embalmer knows it.
The salesman knows it.
It is the oldest upsell in this business, and it gets sold with a straight face to a woman who is crying.
So, line one.
Eleven hundred and ninety-five dollars.
Not eight thousand.
Not four.
Eleven ninety-five.
Tonight, before you go to sleep, if you have a funeral home in mind, your mothers, your grandmothers, the one down the street, Call them and
ask one question.
Can I bring my own casket?
If they hesitate, you have your answer about the rest of the list too.
Line 2.
The hole.
In Texas and in most of this country, the cemetery will not let you put a casket in the ground by itself.
They require an outer container, a grave liner, or a bolt.
And this is where a family that was careful with the casket gets taken on the ground.
A liner is a concrete box with no bottom.
It holds the earth so the grave doesn't sink.
In San Antonio, a liner runs around $1,000 to $1,400.
A vault is a sealed concrete box, sometimes lined, sometimes with a lid that locks, and it runs $2,500 to $3,500.
The difference between them, in the ground, after 20 years, is nothing you will ever see.
The cemetery requires a container.
It does not require the expensive one.
That's the cemetery's rule, not the law.
I asked a cemetery manager on Sarsamora, a man named Ruben.
This was maybe 15 years ago.
I asked him straight out, Ruben, what did you put on your own, mother?
He looked at me and he said, the liner.
And then he sold balls all day.
My line too, the liner, $1,100.
And I want it bought from a third party, not from the cemetery.
Because the cemetery's price is not the only price.
Ask for two quotes, you're allowed.
And the hall itself, the opening and closing, the interment fee, that's separate.
And that's the cemetery's price, not the funeral homes.
In San Antonio, a weekday grave opening runs around 1,200.
Saturday costs more.
Ask.
Nobody asks.
Line 3.
The embalming.
I'm going to say this slowly because I have had this argument at the arrangement table for 40 years and I have never once lost it.
The FTC funeral requires every funeral home in this country to tell you in writing that embalming is not required by law in most cases.
Not required.
They hand you a piece of paper that says it and then they say the word recommended and your hands go cold and you sign.
Texas does not require embalming.
What Texas requires is that the body be kept cool until the burial.
That's it.
Refrigeration in a funeral home costs about $350 for a few days.
Embalming costs $700 to $1,000, depending on the home.
Now, I am not against embalming.
If a family wants an open casket, if they want three days of visitation, if they want to see their mother's face one more time and
touch her hand, then embalm her.
And don't let anybody make you feel cheap for it.
That's not cheap.
That's love.
And it has a price and it's a fair price.
But that is not what I want for me.
I want the lid closed.
I want my family to remember me at the kitchen table with a cup of coffee and my reading glasses pushed up on my head.
Not in a box under a light.
Closed casket.
Refrigeration.
No embalming. $350.
And I'll tell you why and this is the part I don't say at the arrangement table.
My father's face, the last time I saw it, is not the face I want in my son's head for the rest of his life.
I want him to keep the other one, the one at the table.
That's the one I'm leaving him.
Line four, the room.
Here is where Mexican families and American funeral homes want completely different things, and nobody translates.
An American funeral home will sell you a chapel.
The facility use fee, that's the room, $300 to $800.
A staff for service fee, another $300 to $500.
A visitation fee per day.
By the time you finish the list, you have paid $2,000 for a room with carpet and a podium.
I am not paying for a room.
My funeral is at San Fernando Cemetery number 2, at the graveside under the mesquite trees where the sun comes through at 4 in the afternoon,
and the rosary is at my house in the living room with the kitchen full.
You want to know the real difference between a Mexican wake and an American one?
In the American one, the family sits in a row and people come to them.
In the Mexican one, the family is in the kitchen making coffee for everybody.
The aunts are arguing about the tamales, somebody's kid is asleep on the coach, the neighbor brings a pot of café de hoja and doesn't say
anything, just sets it down and leaves.
That room costs nothing.
That room is the whole thing.
Now, before I go on, I want you to do something.
Take out your phone, not later, now.
Search for the funeral home your family would call if if something happened to you tonight.
The one three streets over, the one you're unused.
Pull up their website and find their general price list.
The federal rule says it has to be there.
Time yourself.
60 seconds.
If you can't find it in 60 seconds, that's the first thing you learned today and it didn't cost you anything.
If you do find it, take a screenshot and send it to the person who would have to make these decisions, not to scare them, so
that when the phone rings at 2 in the morning, they are not opening a website for the first time.
Okay.
You can put the phone down, but keep the screenshot.
Line 5.
The ground.
I bought two plots in 2004, San Fernando Cemetery No.
2, on the west side. $1,400 each, and I paid the perpetual care on top of it.
That's the fund the cemetery keeps to cut the grass forever.
In Texas, a perpetual care cemetery has to hold that money somewhere separate.
Check your contract for it.
If they can't tell you where the perpetual care money goes, walk.
Two plots, one for Rosa, one for me.
Rosa and I have been married 34 years.
She's a hospice chaplain.
She has sat with more dying people than I have buried, and she has opinions about all of this, and she is usually right.
Now listen to me, because this is the line where I have seen the most damage.
The plot is real estate.
Buy the plot.
Do not prepay the funeral.
Prepaid funeral contracts are a different animal.
The FTC funeral rule does not cover them.
That's the thing nobody tells you.
The rule that protects you at the arrangement table does not protect you when you sign a prepaid contract 10 years early.
In Texas, they're regulated by the Department of Insurance, and every seller has to be permitted.
Ask for the permit number.
If they can't give it to you, you're not talking to a funeral home.
You're talking to a salesman.
I saw a family in 2011, a woman from Laredo.
Her name was Ophelia.
She had paid $11,000 in 1998 for her husband's funeral in installments over eight years.
When he died, the funeral home told her the contract covered a casket that no longer existed, and the difference was $4,000 due at the door.
She paid it.
She had no choice.
That's not a funeral.
That's a trap with a payment plan.
Buy the ground.
Keep the money in your own account.
Put a note in the folder that says what you want.
That's the prepayment I recommend and it costs nothing.
Line 6.
The list of small things.
This is the part that doesn't show up in anybody's video and it's where $400 at a time the bill goes from $6,000 to $9,000.
Every general price list has a page of what they call merchandise and services.
Here's what's on the one from the home on Guadalupe Street, and I have seen the same list in 20 cities.
A registered book.
The book people sign. $95.
I can buy the same book at the office supply store for $12.
A hundred acknowledgement cards. $65.
Nobody sends them anymore.
Nobody.
A memorial package.
The folders, the prayer cards, the laminated bookmark with the 23rd Psalm.
The print shop on Commerce does the same cards for 80.
A limousine for the family. $350.
In San Antonio, the cemetery is 11 minutes from the church.
A casket spray. $400 from the funeral homes florist.
The Mercado on Sarzamora does it for 120 and it is bigger.
A crucifix rental.
I am not making this up.
Fifty dollars.
A rental for a cross.
None of that is in my four lines.
Not one.
My son Rafa can buy the registered book at Walmart on the way and my granddaughter can pick the flowers at the market, and nobody at
that gravesite is going to look around and say, this funeral was missing the laminated bookmark.
The rule here is simple.
The price list is not a menu where you have to order the combination.
It's a list.
You point at what you want, you say no to the rest, and they have to give it to you itemized.
That's the whole law.
That's what 1984 was for.
Now parking lot stuff, the paperwork, nobody talks about this part and it's the part that keeps a family up at night for six months after
everybody has gone home.
You are going to need death certificates, certified copies.
The funeral home orders them for you and charges $20 to $25 each and they will tell you to get 10, get 12.
You need one for the bank, one for each insurance policy, one for the title company, one for the mortgage, one for Social Security, one for
the pension, one for the credit union, and one you keep with your own papers forever in a plastic sleeve, because you will lose the others.
In Bexar County, you can order them yourself from the county clerk once the funeral home files the certificate for less than half that price.
It takes about three weeks.
You have three weeks.
Nobody is going to die from the wait.
The disposition permit is the paper that lets the cemetery open the ground.
The funeral home files it.
You don't file anything.
But you do have to sign it.
And Rafa, this part is for you.
You sign it where it says informant and you don't let anybody hurry you through it and you read the name on it out loud before
you put the pen down.
I have seen a wrong name on a permit.
I have seen it twice in 40 years.
Both times it was a family that was rushed.
And Social Security.
The funeral home used to report the deaths for the family.
Many still will.
Many won't.
And nobody tells you which kind you have.
So ask at the arrangement table, are you going to report these deaths to Social Security for me and will you give me the confirmation?
If the answer is no, you call yourself and you have 30 days to return the last payment.
There is also a $255 desk benefit and a payment that has to go back.
Both of those get missed by families who are grieving, and both of them cost money.
Write it on the paper.
On the back, who calls Social Security?
Line 7.
The names.
A funeral is not a product.
It's a set of jobs, and somebody has to do each one, and if nobody is named, the funeral home names somebody and charges you for
it.
So I wrote names on my paper.
Rafa signs the disposition permit and talks to the cemetery.
He's 41 and he runs the funeral home now and he is going to want to upgrade something.
He's my son, he's going to want to do right by me.
Rosa has my permission to hit him with a rolled up newspaper.
Lalo carries the head.
Lalo is 26.
He's been with us two years and he's the one who is going to be nervous.
So I want him in the front on the left where I can see him if I could see him.
My granddaughter Itzel reads the poem.
She's 19 and she writes and she'll pick something that will ruin everybody.
And that is her job.
And Rosa does the talking at the graveside.
Not a hired officiant.
Not a stranger with a nice voice who never met me.
My wife.
She has done it for other families for 34 years.
She can do it for me.
That's four names.
Write the names.
If a name is missing, a stranger fills it, and you pay for the stranger.
Line 8.
The music.
At my graveside there will be a mariachi, three men, maybe four, from the west side, and they will play Amor Eterno, and they will be
paid four hundred dollars in cash, and they will be worth every dollar of it.
I know exactly what that song does at a grave.
I have watched it do it a hundred times.
The widows who have held it together through the whole rosary, through the whole mass, through the whole walk from the car, and then the trumpet
starts and they break.
That's the point of it.
Some things are supposed to break.
And here is why that song, for me.
November 2nd, 1999.
My father was 71, and he had a cane, and he walked the whole Mesquitan with me.
He lit a candle for my grandmother, his mother, at her grave, and he sat there on the edge of the stone, and he did not
want to leave.
It got dark.
The families were still there.
The mariachi were playing three graves over, and at two in the morning, my father grabbed my arm and said, ¿Ya sabes donde está el papel
de esta tumba?
Do you know where the paper for this grave is?
Two in the morning, in the dark, and that's what he's worried about, the paper, the refrendo, whether the grave was paid.
We found the paper.
It was in the glove box of his truck, in a yellow folder, folded in three.
And the mariachi played Amor Eterno while we were standing there, and my father sang the two lines he knew and hummed the rest.
The next morning, the ground was yellow with Sempa Súchil, and he was still there.
And we walked out together, and at the gate he stopped and he said, mijo, cuando me toque a mí, when it's my turn, and he
told me four things.
Standing at the gate of the Mesquitan on the morning of November 3rd, 1999, my father told me what he wanted for his own funeral.
I wrote it on the back of the refrendo receipt.
I still have it.
He died in 2003, in the spring.
I was in San Antonio, and I flew down, and we did exactly what he said.
The mariachi, the $400, the amor eterno, all of it.
My brother thought I was showing off.
It wasn't for them.
It was the last thing my father asked me for, and I had it written down, so I did not have to guess.
That's what the paper is for, not the money.
The paper is so you don't have to guess at the worst moment of your life.
Line nine.
What goes in?
Everybody thinks about this one and everybody is a little embarrassed to ask.
I'll tell you what goes in mine.
The rosary my mother gave me when I made my first communion.
It's been in a drawer for 50 years and it's got a chip on the fourth bead, a packet of soil from Enelco.
My sister will bring it in a plastic bag in her purse from the yard behind the funeral home on the corner where my father swept
the sidewalk every morning at six and where I swept it after him.
A letter from Rosa.
She doesn't know I wrote this down, but she's going to write it.
And a photograph of my father from 1958 in front of the door of the funeral home with the sign that he painted himself.
Nothing else.
No jewelry.
No watch.
No shoes.
My son has my shoes.
He's got the same size and is welcome to them.
No money.
I have buried men with a roll of bills in their jacket pocket and I have never once believed it did anything for them.
And here is the rule I would give anybody.
Put in the box only what is a message, not what is valuable.
If it's valuable, it's a gift and gifts are for the living.
The box gets the message.
Before I read you the last line, I want to ask you for something and then I'll never mention it again.
If you've stayed with me this long, you're the kind of person who thinks about this and I'm glad you're here.
Subscribe and tell me in the comments where your family is from and how they do it there.
Because I read them, all of them, and I have learned more about this country from those comments than from any book.
That's the trade.
You give me your town, I give you 40 years.
Okay?
Line 10.
The four lines on my paper are these.
The box, $11.95.
The liner, $11.00.
The refrigeration, $3.50.
The mariachi, $4.00.
The plot, already paid, $2,004. $1,400.
The flowers from the market, the register book from Walmart, my granddaughter's poem, $150.
The cemetery's opening and closing, $1,200.
The permit and the death certificates, about $100, $4,810.
That's my funeral.
40 years, 7,000 burials, and that's the number.
Not 11,000, not the number Mrs.
Delgado was quoted on the phone that day in 2007, the one where I show her three things and she walk out paying half.
The same three things, the box, the liner, and the list of small things, and none of it, not one dollar of it, is a mystery
to my family, because it's on a piece of paper in my wallet and a copy in the folder in the desk drawer, in the second
drawer under the phone book.
Here's what I want you to do tonight.
It takes 20 minutes.
Get a piece of paper.
Write four lines.
Who does the talking?
Where the body goes?
What goes in the box?
And how much you're willing to spend?
A number, not a filling.
Put your name and the date at the tab.
Fold it.
Put it in your wallet or in the drawer where your family keeps the papers.
And then do the thing that most people never do.
Tell one person where it is.
The funeral is not for the person in the box.
I've said that to a thousand families.
The funeral is for the people in the chairs.
And the kindest thing you can do for the people in the chairs is to not make them guess.
I'm Ernie Navarro.
40 years.
I'll see you at the next one.
And next time, I'm going to tell you what I found in 2015, when we opened the grave at San Fernando after 10 years, what was
left and what wasn't, and why the salesman who sold that family a protective casket should have been ashamed of himself.
You're going to want to see it.
I'll be here.
